gpt.rationale: A landlord must give a residential tenant who defaults under the lease at least three days’ written notice to vacate before filing a forcible detainer action. The statute allows a written lease or agreement to provide a shorter or longer notice period.

gemini.rationale: A landlord must give a tenant who defaults on rent at least three days' written notice to vacate the premises before the landlord files a forcible detainer suit. This statutory period can be modified if the parties have contracted for a shorter or longer notice period in a written lease.

notice_defects.note: Notice must be served by a legally recognized method — verify statutory service requirements for this state
Notice must provide minimum 3 day(s) — verify calculation method

method_rules.requirements: In-person delivery to tenant or occupant 16+ at premises
Regular mail to premises; 3 additional days added to notice period
Affixing notice to main entry door of premises

federal.name: CARES Act §4024
federal.applies_when: Covered dwelling: federally backed mortgage loan (Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac) or covered housing program (HUD assistance, Section 8, LIHTC, rural housing, etc.)
federal.effect: During active moratorium periods: 30-day notice required before filing; no fees or penalties for nonpayment during moratorium. Emergency moratorium provisions expired July 2021 but covered-dwelling definition and notice requirements may persist under other federal programs — verify current applicability.

state_protective.name: Implied Warranty of Habitability
state_protective.effect: Landlord must make repairs affecting health and safety; tenant may repair-and-deduct up to one month's rent if landlord fails to repair in 7 days after notice

state_protective.name: Anti-Retaliation
state_protective.effect: Landlord may not retaliate against tenant for good-faith exercise of rights; presumption of retaliation if adverse action within 6 months

local.effect: Austin has limited additional tenant protections; verify current ordinances — state law preempts most rent control
local.digitization_note: Texas state law preempts local rent control ordinances (Tex. Prop. Code §214.902)

elements: Landlord knew or had notice of the defect
Defect substantially impairs habitability (health, safety, or welfare)
Tenant gave landlord reasonable time to repair
Tenant did not cause or waive the defect
substantive_defenses.note: Habitability warranty statute: Tex. Prop. Code §92.052. Elements, available remedies (rent withholding, repair-and-deduct, rent escrow), and applicability as a defense to eviction vary significantly by state — attorney verification required. Statute identified via machine-assisted retrieval — attorney verification required before use

elements: Tenant engaged in protected activity (habitability complaint, union organizing, exercising legal rights)
Landlord knew of the protected activity
Adverse action (eviction, rent increase, service reduction) followed protected activity
Causal connection between protected activity and adverse action
Action was within state-defined presumption period (varies: 60 days to 12 months)
substantive_defenses.note: Anti-retaliation statute: Tex. Prop. Code §92.331. Presumption period, protected activities, and available remedies vary by state — attorney verification required. Statute identified via machine-assisted retrieval — attorney verification required before use

elements: Tenant is member of a protected class (race, color, national origin, sex, disability, familial status, religion — per federal FHA; state law may add classes)
Similarly situated non-protected tenants were treated more favorably, OR discriminatory intent can be shown, OR facially neutral policy has disparate impact
substantive_defenses.statute: 42 U.S.C. §3604 (Fair Housing Act); Tex. Prop. Code §301.003
substantive_defenses.note: Federal FHA prohibits discrimination in housing based on protected class. State law may provide additional protected classes and remedies. Discriminatory intent or disparate impact analysis is fact-intensive — specialist review required. grounding_gap: state fair housing case law and protected class details.

elements: Tenant had a valid lease or tenancy
Landlord substantially interfered with tenant's right to peaceful possession
substantive_defenses.note: Breach of covenant of quiet enjoyment — primarily common law doctrine in most states; some states codify at RLTA. grounding_gap: whether state recognizes as affirmative defense to eviction, constructive eviction standard, and remedies vary — specialist review required.

elements: Amount demanded in notice exceeds lawfully owed rent
Impermissible charges included (late fees, utilities, damages, other non-rent items)
substantive_defenses.note: Improper rent calculation — relevant where landlord has included improper charges (late fees, fees not authorized by lease) in the rent demand. grounding_gap: state-specific rules on what may be included in rent demand, and whether overcharge voids notice — specialist review required.

procedural_defects.consequence: Unlawful detainer action is premature; court lacks jurisdiction; may be dismissed
procedural_defects.note: Filing before the notice period runs is a bright-line defect in most states

procedural_defects.consequence: Court lacks subject matter jurisdiction; case must be dismissed or transferred

procedural_defects.consequence: Complaint defective; may be dismissed or require amendment
